fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/summary: Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–c. 395), Basil’s younger brother, was the most philosophically creative of the Cappadocians: defender of Nicene Trinitarian theology against Eunomius, theorist of God’s infinity and of endless spiritual progress (epektasis), and an advocate of the final restoration of all.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/story:
Gregory was born around 335, a younger brother of Basil and Macrina. He was educated largely at home and by Basil, whom he called his ‘teacher’, and for a time worked as a rhetor, apparently married (his wife is sometimes identified with a Theosebeia mentioned by Gregory of Nazianzus). His treatise On Virginity (c. 371), praising the ascetic life, laments that he himself had not chosen it.

Around 372 Basil made him bishop of the small town of Nyssa as part of his struggle against Valens. Basil found him naïve in church politics, and in 376 Homoian opponents had him deposed on charges of financial irregularity; he returned in 378 after Valens’ death. After Basil’s death in 379 Gregory emerged as a leading figure in his own right: he attended the Council of Antioch (379), visited his dying sister Macrina, whose deathbed conversation he recast as the dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection, played a major role at the Council of Constantinople (381), and was named by Theodosius as one of the bishops in communion with whom orthodoxy was defined. He preached at the funeral of Meletius and later of the Empress Flacilla, and travelled to Arabia and Jerusalem, returning critical of pilgrimage (Letter 2).

His Against Eunomius (380–383) completed Basil’s refutation of the Neo-Arian claim that the divine essence can be known and named as ‘unbegotten’. Gregory argued that God is infinite (apeiron) and therefore beyond every concept; names indicate God’s activities (energeiai), not his essence. To Ablabius explains why Father, Son and Spirit are not ‘three gods’: their single activity proceeds from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. The Catechetical Oration (c. 385) is a systematic handbook for teachers, including the ‘fish-hook’ image of the atonement, in which the devil is deceived by Christ’s humanity.

In later works, The Life of Moses and the Homilies on the Song of Songs, he described the soul’s journey into the ‘luminous darkness’ of God as never-ending: because God is infinite, perfection consists in constant growth (epektasis, from Philippians 3:13). On the Making of Man interprets the image of God as freedom and royal dignity shared by all human beings, and his fourth Homily on Ecclesiastes contains one of antiquity’s most radical condemnations of slavery. With Origen, he hoped that evil, being finite, would finally be exhausted and all creatures restored to God.

After centuries in the shadow of Basil and Nazianzen, Gregory was rediscovered in the twentieth century by Jean Daniélou, Hans Urs von Balthasar and Werner Jaeger’s critical edition, and is now one of the most studied Fathers.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/roots/0/text: Deeply Origenist in exegesis, spirituality and eschatology; formed by Basil and by the ascetic teaching of his sister Macrina, whom he calls ‘the Teacher’.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/roots/1/text: His ascent of the soul, the language of participation and the image of God as mirror reflect Plotinus, while his doctrine of divine infinity and endless progress departs from the Neoplatonic goal of rest.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/roots/2/text: The Life of Moses follows Philo’s Life of Moses in structure and allegory, reinterpreted christologically.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/roots/3/text: Uses Aristotelian and Stoic logic of universals in To Ablabius and Against Eunomius, while warning against Eunomius’ ‘technical’ logic.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/roots/4/text: A former professional rhetor whose writing shows the training of the Second Sophistic.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/roots/5/text: Wrote On Virginity and the Life of Macrina, and his mystical works address monastic readers.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/keyTeachings/0: God is infinite and incomprehensible; we know God by his activities, not his essence
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/keyTeachings/1: Epektasis: the soul’s eternal, endless progress into God
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/keyTeachings/2: Father, Son and Spirit share a single activity, so there are not three gods
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/keyTeachings/3: The image of God belongs to humanity as a whole, expressed in freedom and dignity
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/keyTeachings/4: Condemnation of slavery as contrary to the image of God
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/keyTeachings/5: Hope for the restoration of all (apokatastasis) when evil is exhausted
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/0/note: Major defence of Nicene theology and divine infinity.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/1/title: To Ablabius: That There Are Not Three Gods
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/1/note: Short treatise on unity and distinction in the Trinity.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/3/note: Completion of Basil’s Hexaemeron, on human nature.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/4/title: On the Soul and the Resurrection
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/4/note: Dialogue with Macrina modelled on Plato’s Phaedo.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/5/note: Mystical ascent of Sinai as a model of Christian perfection.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/6/title: Homilies on the Song of Songs
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/works/6/note: Fifteen homilies, a classic of mystical theology.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/doctrineContrib: Developed the arguments for unity of activity and distinction of persons that secured the Cappadocian settlement.
Founder of apophatic mystical theology: the ‘luminous darkness’ and endless progress.
The most explicit patristic advocate of universal restoration after Origen, never formally condemned.
A theology of the image of God as universal human dignity, including a rare ancient critique of slavery.
The ‘fish-hook’ ransom image in the Catechetical Oration.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/laterInfluence/: His apophaticism and theology of the divine activities passed into Pseudo-Dionysius and Maximus the Confessor.
His distinction between God’s essence and activities underlies the later essence–energies theology.
Eriugena translated and transmitted him; through Dionysius he shaped medieval mysticism.
Rediscovered by Daniélou, von Balthasar and Sarah Coakley; invoked in modern discussions of universalism, gender and the critique of slavery.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/reception/0/tex: Honoured as ‘father of fathers’ by the Second Council of Nicaea (787); feast 10 January.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/reception/1/tex: Saint and Father (feast 10 January), though not a Doctor of the Church.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/reception/2/tex: Revered as one of the Cappadocian Fathers.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/reception/3/tex: Valued in academic theology and by universalists; his apokatastasis is debated among evangelicals.
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/controversies/0: Deposition in 376 on charges of financial mismanagement
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/controversies/1: His hope for universal restoration and whether it was ‘Origenist’
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/controversies/2: Debates on the ‘double creation’ of humanity and gender in On the Making of Man
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/controversies/3: Critique of pilgrimage to Jerusalem in Letter 2, later used by Protestants
fathers/gregory-of-nyssa/quote/text: This truly is the vision of God: never to be satisfied in the desire to see him.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/summary: Roman aristocrat and provincial governor (c. 339–397) acclaimed bishop of Milan in 374 while still unbaptised, who defeated the Homoian (Arian) party in the West, faced down emperors, brought Greek theology and Philo into Latin, wrote the first Latin congregational hymns and baptised Augustine.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/story:
Ambrose was born around 339 at Trier, where his father served as praetorian prefect of the Gauls. After his father’s death the family moved to Rome, where he received the full education of a senatorial son in literature, rhetoric, law and Greek. He practised as an advocate at Sirmium and around 370 was appointed governor (consularis) of Aemilia-Liguria, with his seat at Milan, then the main imperial residence in the West.

When the Homoian bishop Auxentius died in 374, the election of his successor threatened to become violent. Ambrose went to the church to keep order and, according to his biographer Paulinus, a child’s cry of ‘Ambrose bishop!’ was taken up by the crowd. Though only a catechumen, he was baptised and consecrated within a week (traditionally 7 December 374). He gave away his property, and under the guidance of the priest Simplician threw himself into the study of Scripture and the Greek theologians — Origen, Didymus, Basil and Athanasius — and of the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria.

Ambrose turned Milan into a stronghold of Nicene faith. He wrote On the Faith (378–380) for the young emperor Gratian, engineered the deposition of Homoian bishops at the Council of Aquileia (381), and opposed the restoration of the Altar of Victory in the Senate house demanded by the pagan senator Symmachus (384). In 385–386 he refused the empress-mother Justina’s demand that a basilica be handed to the Homoians, occupying it with his congregation, who passed the vigil singing his new hymns. In 386 he discovered the relics of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and placed them under the altar of his new basilica, a decisive moment in the Western cult of relics.

His relations with Theodosius I show both his courage and his limits. In 388 he forced the emperor to withdraw an order that the bishop of Callinicum rebuild a synagogue burnt by Christians — an intervention now widely criticised. In 390, after Theodosius’s troops massacred thousands in the circus at Thessalonica, Ambrose wrote demanding public penance, and the emperor submitted. ‘The emperor is within the Church, not above it’ became a charter of ecclesiastical independence in the West.

Ambrose’s preaching drew the young professor of rhetoric Augustine, who heard him expound the Old Testament allegorically and lost his Manichaean objections to it; Ambrose baptised him at the Easter Vigil of 387. His De officiis adapted Cicero’s ethics for clergy, his De sacramentis and De mysteriis are key witnesses to fourth-century initiation and Eucharistic belief, and four hymns certainly his — including Aeterne rerum conditor and Veni redemptor gentium — founded the Latin hymn tradition. He died on Holy Saturday, 4 April 397.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/roots/0/text: Trained as an advocate and governor, he brought administrative skill and a jurist’s sense of authority and precedent to episcopal office and to his dealings with the court.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/roots/1/text: His De officiis follows Cicero’s De officiis book by book, Christianising Roman ideas of duty, the honestum and the utile.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/roots/2/text: His treatises on Paradise, Cain and Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Joseph draw so heavily on Philo’s allegories that they are a main witness to Philo’s text; he was Philo’s chief conduit into Latin.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/roots/3/text: Pierre Courcelle and Pierre Hadot showed that sermons such as On Isaac and On the Good of Death borrow passages from Plotinus’s Enneads — the Christian Platonism that helped convert Augustine.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/roots/4/text: His Hexaemeron adapts Basil’s homilies, his On the Holy Spirit depends on Didymus and Basil, and his exegesis follows Origen.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/roots/5/text: Through Cicero (and behind him Panaetius) he took over Stoic frameworks of the cardinal virtues and natural duties, which he reinterpreted biblically.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/roots/6/text: Bishop of the imperial residence, he was adviser and opponent to Gratian, Valentinian II and Theodosius, and defined the Western idea of the Church’s freedom from the emperor.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/keyTeachings/0: Nicene faith in the full divinity of the Son and the Spirit against the Homoians
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/keyTeachings/1: The emperor as a son of the Church, subject to its moral discipline (‘within the Church, not above it’)
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/keyTeachings/2: Sacramental realism: the words of Christ change the elements into his body and blood
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/keyTeachings/3: The excellence of consecrated virginity and Mary as model of virgins and type of the Church
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/keyTeachings/4: Christian duty and social justice: the earth was given to all in common, and almsgiving restores to the poor what is theirs (On Naboth)
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/keyTeachings/5: Spiritual exegesis of the Old Testament, which unlocked Scripture for Augustine
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/0/title: On the Faith (De fide), to Gratian
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/0/note: Five books defending the divinity of the Son against the Homoians.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/1/note: Three books on the divinity of the Spirit, drawing on Didymus and Basil.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/2/title: On the Duties of Ministers (De officiis)
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/2/note: A Christian rewriting of Cicero’s De officiis, the first Latin manual of Christian ethics.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/3/title: On the Sacraments and On the Mysteries
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/3/note: Post-baptismal catecheses explaining baptism, chrismation and the Eucharist; De sacramentis preserves an early form of the Roman canon.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/4/note: Sermons on the six days of creation, adapted from Basil.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/5/note: Four authenticated by Augustine’s testimony (Aeterne rerum conditor, Deus creator omnium, Iam surgit hora tertia, Veni redemptor gentium); many more ‘Ambrosian’ hymns imitate them.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/6/title: Letters and the Exposition of the Gospel of Luke
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/works/6/note: The letters include those on the Altar of Victory, Callinicum and Thessalonica; the Luke commentary is his longest exegetical work.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/doctrineContrib: Secured Nicene orthodoxy in northern Italy and the Latin West and transmitted Greek pro-Nicene theology to Latin readers.
His catecheses give a strong realist account of the Eucharist (the ‘word of Christ’ effects a change) that later fed into medieval Eucharistic theology.
His confrontations with emperors established the Western principle that rulers are subject to the Church’s moral judgement.
Introduced antiphonal psalmody and metrical hymn-singing to the West; the Ambrosian rite of Milan bears his name.
Promoted consecrated virginity, Marian piety and the cult of martyrs’ relics, notably Gervasius and Protasius.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/laterInfluence/: His preaching, Christian Platonism and baptism of Augustine made him the decisive human influence on the most important Latin Father.
Counted with Jerome, Augustine and Gregory as one of the four Latin Doctors (formally from 1298); his stance with Theodosius was cited in medieval church–state disputes.
Luther translated Veni redemptor gentium as ‘Nun komm, der Heiden Heiland’; Reformers cited him against later Roman claims and on justification by faith (texts later shown to be Ambrosiaster).
The Ambrosian rite survives in the archdiocese of Milan; his hymns remain in the Divine Office and in hymnals of many traditions.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/reception/0/tex: One of the four great Latin Doctors; feast 7 December; patron of Milan and of beekeepers.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/reception/1/tex: Commemorated on 7 December as a holy hierarch and defender of Nicene faith.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/reception/2/tex: Commemorated in calendars and widely sung; cited by the Reformers as a witness to the faith of the early Church.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/reception/3/tex: His Callinicum letter, defending Christians who burnt a synagogue, is cited as an early example of state-backed anti-Judaism.
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/controversies/0: The Callinicum affair (388): pressuring Theodosius to cancel compensation for a burnt synagogue
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/controversies/1: His use of popular pressure and relics in the basilica conflict with Justina (385–386)
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/controversies/2: The Altar of Victory dispute (384) with Symmachus over the place of traditional Roman religion
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/controversies/3: His heavy dependence on Philo, Plotinus and Basil, which older scholars treated as plagiarism and recent scholars as creative adaptation
fathers/ambrose-of-milan/quote/text: The emperor is within the Church, not above the Church.
